analysis.one_liner: Charges a 20% tax when high earners borrow against assets like stocks instead of selling them.
analysis.headline: The bill sits untouched in the House Ways and Means Committee, with one sponsor and 11 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no committee action since its December 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: Wealthy households can borrow against appreciated assets like stocks or art without selling them, so they never report the gains as income and never pay income tax on them. This bill would charge such borrowers a 20% tax each year on the amount they borrow against those assets, if they earn over $400,000 a year ($450,000 for couples). Home mortgages, home equity loans, margin loans, and farm loans are excluded. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise subsidize a system where the wealthiest households can live off asset-backed borrowing indefinitely without paying income tax on their gains; federal revenue would rise, though the bill does not specify how it would be spent.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 20% excise tax, paid by the borrower, on amounts borrowed each year under a loan or credit line secured by capital assets when the borrower earns over $400,000 ($450,000 joint) [S2].
Targets the strategy by which people with large unrealized gains borrow against those assets instead of selling, avoiding income tax because no sale occurs [S2].

Excludes home mortgages, home equity loans, margin loans, and loans secured by farmland, so the tax reaches asset-backed borrowing by high earners without touching most household or farm borrowing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: High-income households with large investment, business, or collectible assets who want liquidity without selling them, and any lender or wealth adviser whose business depends on arranging such loans.

drawbacks.text: A 20% tax on every dollar borrowed is steep and applies regardless of the borrower's purpose, so legitimate liquidity needs — a business owner raising cash against company assets, an investor refinancing — pay the same rate as tax avoidance [S2].
Because the tax is on borrowing rather than income, it can be avoided by not borrowing, meaning it does not tax the underlying gains directly and leaves the unrealized-income issue unresolved [S2].
The bill gives the Treasury Secretary broad authority to write the rules, so the practical line between taxed and untaxed borrowing would depend on regulations not yet written [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is sound in targeting a gap where the largest gains in the economy go untaxed because no sale happens. But the design is blunt: a flat 20% tax on borrowing rather than a tax on the gain itself will also hit high earners who borrow for ordinary business or liquidity reasons, and the richest households can most easily sidestep it by adjusting their borrowing arrangements. As written, it would raise money from a group that currently pays little on unrealized gains, but a more tailored version could reach the same avoidance with fewer side effects.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2025, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and has received no hearings, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Goldman introduced the bill on December 4, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S4].
Eleven other House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors appear on the list [S3].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, high-income households using asset-backed borrowing and the lenders and wealth-advisers who arrange it are better off than they would be under the bill, since the status quo continues while it sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asset-backed borrowers and their lenders, so far

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors are House Democrats, and no Republicans are on the cosponsor list [S3].

industries.industry: High-net-worth households and their wealth advisers
industries.note: These households use loans secured by stocks and other assets to generate spendable cash without selling and triggering income tax; the 20% tax directly cuts into that strategy. Their interest runs against the broader taxpayer's here.

Lenders that arrange securities-based and asset-backed credit for wealthy clients would face reduced demand as borrowing becomes 20% more expensive, though mortgages, margin loans, and farmland loans are excluded. Ordinary consumer and mortgage lending is untouched.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that go to Ways and Means with one-party sponsorship and no committee action in their first weeks rarely reach the floor; the realistic path is that it stays parked unless tax policy becomes a priority, possibly as an ingredient in a larger tax bill someone else writes.
